extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history and philosophy of science (readers studying Bacon's influence and scientific method)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the principles, strengths, limitations, and historical influence of Francis Bacon's proposed scientific method (Novum Organum), especially its emphasis on induction and experimental practice, and how that method informed later natural philosophy and moral/political thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baconian induction (primary aim of logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'new Logic' whose principal end is to show the manner of making a good Induction — induction as the principal aim of the new logic rather than syllogistic demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Novum Organum 'teaches a new Logic, whose principal aim is to show the manner of making a good Induction, as the principal end of Logic.' Induction should be systematic and aimed at discovery, not merely at rhetorical assent. (Cf. Journal des Savans on the Novum Organum.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method (empirical observation and experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge should be sought by experiment and observation — the experimental or inductive method is central to arriving at knowledge of nature and its effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple testimonies (Descartes, Mersenne, Gassendi, Sorbiere, Voltaire, Condillac, Comenius, etc.) characterize Bacon as proposing experimental philosophy: 'the Father of experimental philosophy' and urging that experiments be made and reported. Practical, repeated experiments and careful description of appearances are required (e.g., Descartes' letters noting 'useful experiments' and invitations to 'describe the heavens exactly' without hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic should test first principles (test the principia themselves)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the business of the new method/logic to test the first principles (principia scientiarum) themselves, rather than rely on syllogistic forms which merely secure assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using syllogism as the tool of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogism is more proper for attaining victory in dispute than for discovery or confirmation of truth; fallacies can be couched in syllogisms, so discovery requires something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke and other quoted passages echo the idea: 'Syllogism has been thought more proper for the attaining Victory in Dispute, than for the Discovery or Confirmation of Truth in fair enquiries.' Thus one should not treat syllogistic logic as sufficient for forming new scientific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose and remove idols (causes of error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the common sources of error (idola) in human understanding and take them into account when forming methods of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spinoza and others discuss Bacon's 'Idola' (Idola Tribus) and his attention to causes of error: 'Personne n'a mieux connu que lui la cause de nos erreurs.' The method includes a critique of the human mind's dispositions that mislead inquiry and prescribes norms to remedy them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply experimental results to practical ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The results of natural philosophy should be reduced to useful practice — applying discoveries to mechanics and the practical difficulties of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sorbiere's testimony: Bacon's work 'reduire utilement en pratique, et tirer hors des disputes de l'Ecole, ce que l'on a de connoissances de la Nature; afin de les appliquer à la mechanique.' The method is praised for its practical orientation: stimulating experiments that can be applied to manufacture, mechanics, and life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction demands sustained, collective, and industrious effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Good inductive work is laborious, often requiring continuous industry over many persons and generations; it is not an instantaneous method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comenius and others emphasize that Baconian induction 'poscit... industriam' and appears 'tum operosa tum a successu quasi incerto suspensa' — i.e., it requires prolonged, cooperative observation and experiment and so may be neglected by those unwilling to undertake sustained effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overclaiming certainty from experimental induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim certain, final knowledge of the general course of nature solely from experiments and observations; be cautious about asserting absolute general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's denial that experiment and observation can lead to certain knowledge regarding the general course of nature is cited as a corrective: even advocates of experiment (and some successors) cautioned against asserting absolute certainty from empirical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Bacon's maxims as heuristic openings rather than fixed formal axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: The propositions and axioms in Bacon's work often function as advisories and expedients to provoke further thought and investigation rather than as fully established principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics (e.g., Baillet on Descartes and commentators on Bacon) observe that some of Bacon's 'propositions and axioms... are rather pieces of advice and expedients to give openings for meditation, than maxims proper for establishing principles.' Treat Bacon's rules as heuristics to guide further empirical work rather than finished doctrines.
